                                      PROJECT NO. 58482

                                                  §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD DEMAND
                                                  §
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE
                                                  §                     OF TEXAS

              VISTRA CORPORATE SERVICES COMPANY’S COMMENTS

       Vistra Corporate Services Company (Vistra) files these Comments in response to the
Proposal for Publication (PFP or Proposed Rule) to adopt new 16 TAC § 25.251. This rulemaking
is to implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 39.170 as enacted by Senate Bill 6 during
the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session. The proposed rule will require ERCOT to ensure that
each electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility
serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol to allow the transmission-voltage
customers to be curtailed during firm load shed; require ERCOT to develop a reliability service to
competitively procure demand reductions from large load customers; and establish a framework
for the program. The Proposed Rule established a comment deadline of September 4, 2026;
therefore, these comments are timely filed. As requested, the executive summary is included in a
separate attachment at the end of the comments.

                                 I.    GENERAL COMMENTS

       Vistra generally disfavors out-of-market capacity programs for demand response in an
energy-only market, where demand should have a natural an intrinsic motivation to avoid market
costs – especially during times of scarcity. The Large Load Demand Management Service
(LLDMS), however, is required by statute so is not optional, and fortunately is at least required to
offset its market-distortive impacts on price formation. Still, it is important to note that LLDMS
inherently provides a duplicative value by providing both a capacity payment (LLDMS
procurement) and the avoided cost of energy while curtailed. While Vistra has concerns with the
potentially duplicated value of LLDMS being incongruent with the rest of the market construct, it
is a statutorily-required program and the competitive single clearing-price procurement should
discipline the clearing price.

       So while Vistra would not typically support establishing this kind of demand response
program in an energy-only market, within the statutory context Vistra observes that the proposed
rule executes on its statutory charge generally well, and Vistra’s substantive comments are focused

Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                 Page 1
 on clarifying and coordinating the proposed rule with other statutory and rule requirements, as well
as practical implementation considerations along four themes:

   •   The curtailment directive in proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(a)(1) should apply to loads not
       already otherwise curtailed and include statutory customer coordination language;

   •   Limited deployments for actual transmission emergencies should be allowed for LLDMS;

   •   Clarify that payments are for the LLDMS clearing price, not the wholesale energy price;
       and

   •   Recover the cost on a fixed, self-leveling $/MWh-basis fee across the year, not on an event
       basis.

                     II.    RESPONSES TO PREAMBLE QUESTIONS

   1. Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
      representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
      subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management
      Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available
      but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be
      compensated some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load
      customer’s availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If
      so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load customer for their availability
      during the LLDMS obligation period?

       Vistra does not oppose providing a limited availability payment to qualified large load
customers that remain available throughout the LLDMS obligation period and successfully satisfy
ERCOT verification requirements, even if ERCOT ultimately does not instruct deployment.
Maintaining availability provides reliability value by preserving ERCOT's ability to access
demand reductions should system conditions deteriorate. The majority of the intrinsic
compensation for LLDMS will likely remain the avoided cost of consumed energy from the actual
deployment, though both the deployed and un-deployed LLDMS load likely undertook real costs
to be operationally ready to deploy (regardless of individual outcomes). Accordingly, any
availability payment should represent a modest share of the market clearing price for LLDMS,
with most compensation reserved for resources that are instructed to curtail and successfully
perform. A performance-weighted design (10-25% availability, 75-90% deployment) best aligns




Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                 Page 2
 with the principle that demand response should be compensated primarily by the avoided cost of
energy.


   2. Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar
      year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

          Vistra supports maintaining the proposed $54 million annual budget cap for the LLDMS.
At this stage, there is significant uncertainty regarding participation levels, clearing prices,
deployment frequency, and the overall reliability value that the program will provide. The
proposed cap strikes an appropriate balance between enabling ERCOT to procure a meaningful
reliability service and protecting consumers from excessive costs during initial implementation.

          The Commission should view the $54 million amount as a maximum expenditure cap
rather than a procurement target. ERCOT should procure only the amount of service necessary to
address identified reliability risks. Maintaining the proposed cap will allow the Commission and
stakeholders to evaluate actual program performance, participation, costs, and reliability benefits
before considering any future budget increases.

          Any proposal to increase the cap should be supported by demonstrated evidence that
additional expenditures would provide incremental and cost-effective reliability benefits to
ERCOT customers.

          Furthermore, as explained in greater detail below, the budget should be accumulated on a
self-leveling annual calendar year basis yielding a predictable $/MWh charge for Qualified
Scheduling Entities (QSEs) and Load Serving Entities (LSEs).


   3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
      far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

          ERCOT should assess anticipated extreme weather conditions and associated reliability
risks on a continual basis using its existing forecasting tools, but the decision to initiate an LLDMS
procurement should occur only when ERCOT determines there is a credible risk of an anticipated
emergency condition that will likely require deployment of the service.

          Consistent with the statutory requirement to provide at least 24 hours' notice, ERCOT
should initiate the auction sufficiently in advance to allow successful participants to prepare for a


Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                  Page 3
 potential curtailment event while minimizing forecast uncertainty. Vistra recommends that
ERCOT conduct the auction approximately 24 to 48 hours before the anticipated deployment
period, with ERCOT retaining the flexibility to update procurement quantities as forecasts evolve.

         A procurement window too far in advance may result in over-procurement or procurement
based on weather forecasts that ultimately do not materialize. Conversely, a procurement
conducted too close to the anticipated event may limit participation and reduce the ability of
qualifying loads to safely prepare for curtailment. A 24-to-48-hour procurement window
appropriately balances forecast accuracy, operational preparedness, and competitive participation.
It would also naturally align with the 48-hour forecast review timeline in the Power Outage Alert
rule (16 TAC § 25.57).


    4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

         Vistra supports allowing ERCOT to deploy LLDMS during actual transmission
emergencies when demand reductions can meaningfully mitigate a material reliability threat.
However, the Commission should ensure that LLDMS remains a targeted emergency reliability
tool and is not used for routine congestion management or as a substitute for transmission planning.
ERCOT should be required to demonstrate that the transmission emergency presents a credible
risk to reliability, that existing operational tools are insufficient to address the condition, and that
any deployment is limited to the scope necessary to mitigate the emergency. This approach
preserves operational flexibility while protecting consumers from unnecessary program costs and
maintaining appropriate market incentives. In the comments below, Vistra recommends that
deployment for transmission emergencies be limited to actual transmission emergencies (and not
include anticipated emergencies).

         If the Commission allows ERCOT to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies, Vistra
advocates for the following guardrails:

    1.      Limit Deployments to Reliability Emergencies: LLDMS should only be used when a
            transmission event creates a credible risk of:

            •   Firm load shed,
            •   Cascading outages,

Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                    Page 4
            •   Voltage instability, or
           •   Other significant reliability concerns.

        It should not be used for routine congestion management or economic dispatch issues.


   2.      Require Use of Existing Tools First: ERCOT should demonstrate that existing
           operational tools are insufficient before deploying LLDMS, including:
           •   Network reconfiguration,
           •   Outage management procedures,
           •   Existing emergency protocols.

        LLDMS should remain a tool of last resort.


   3.      Geographic Targeting: Deployments should be limited to the affected transmission-
           constrained area whenever practical, rather than triggering ERCOT-wide curtailments
           for localized problems.


   4.      Demonstrate Incremental Reliability Value: ERCOT should show that the requested
           demand reduction will materially reduce reliability risk and is not merely replacing
           transmission upgrades, planning activities, or normal operational practices.


   5.      Maintain Transparency: Following a deployment, ERCOT should provide stakeholders
           with:

           •   The nature of the transmission emergency,
           •   The amount of LLDMS procured and deployed,
           •   The reliability benefit achieved, and
           •   Why other tools were insufficient.


   6.      Protect Against Routine Use: The Commission should make clear that transmission
           emergency deployments are intended to be exceptional circumstances, not a recurring
           operational tool. Frequent use could indicate underlying transmission planning or
           infrastructure deficiencies that should be addressed through other processes.

Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                              Page 5
        7.       Preserve Cost Controls: Any transmission-related deployment should remain subject
                to:

                •     The annual program budget cap,
                •     Existing procurement limits, and
                •     Cost-effectiveness considerations.


                          III.     COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC RULE PROVISIONS

a. The curtailment directive in proposed 16 TAC §25.521(a)(1) should apply to loads not
   already otherwise curtailed and include statutory customer coordination language.
            Proposed 16 TAC §25.521(a)(1) implements PURA § 39.170(a), which was part of the
suite of large load policies contained in Senate Bill 6 (SB6). SB6 also included curtailment
provisions directed by ERCOT, including in PURA §§ 37.0561(e),1 39.169(d),2 and 39.170(b).3
These each are designed to elicit some curtailment of a large load in anticipation of or during an
emergency event (but prior to firm load shed), meaning that the load will not be available to curtail
during firm load shed because the load will have already been curtailed or moved to backup.
Therefore, it is unnecessary to create duplicative firm load shed curtailment protocols or equipment
requirements for these large loads.



1
  “The independent organization shall establish a threshold before or during an energy emergency alert at which the
organization may issue reasonable notice that large load customers with on-site backup generating facilities may be
directed to either deploy the customer's on-site backup generating facilities or curtail load. After the independent
organization deploys all available market services, except for frequency responsive services, the independent
organization may direct the applicable electric utility or municipally owned utility to require the large load customer
to either deploy the customer's on-site backup generating facilities or curtail load.”
2
    “...The conditions may include:
            (1) requiring the retail customer who is served behind-the-meter to reduce load during certain events;
            (2) requiring the generation resource to make capacity available to the ERCOT power region during certain
            events; …”
3
    “The rules governing this service must:
            (1) specify the periods when the service may be used to assist with maintaining reliability during extreme
            weather events;
            (2) ensure that the independent organization provides at least a 24-hour notice to large load customers and
            requires each large load to remain curtailed for the duration of the energy emergency alert event or until the
            load can be recalled safely;…”


Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                                     Page 6
        Additionally, the statutory language in PURA § 39.170(a) specifies that “The electric
cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally owned utility shall confer with
the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner.” This is an important
principle captured in statute since it recognizes that a one-size-fits-all approach to load shed is not
always appropriate.

       For that reason, Vistra recommends that proposed 16 TAC §25.521(a)(1) be revised as
follows:

       (a)     Directive to ERCOT.
               (1)     ERCOT must ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission and
               distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-
               voltage customer develops a protocol, including the installation of any
               necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to
               allow the load to be curtailed during firm load shed if not already curtailed.
               The electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or municipally
               owned utility shall confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load
               in a coordinated manner. This subsection applies to a load interconnected after
               December 31, 2025, that is not:


               [no changes]


b. Limited deployments for actual transmission emergencies should be allowed for LLDMS.

       PURA § 39.170(b) specifies that LLDMS must (1) be “competitively procure[d] … to be
deployed in the event of an anticipated emergency condition,” “be used to assist with maintaining
reliability during extreme weather events,” and “remain curtailed for the duration of the energy
emergency alert event or until the load can be recalled safely.” While this language does reference
Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) as a metric for deployment, and that is the most probable scenario
in which ERCOT would likely deploy LLDMS, there are also firm load shed risks that emanate
from transmission emergencies – though transmission emergencies may not always result from
extreme weather conditions.

       If loads in ERCOT will be paying into a capacity market for LLDMS, it is reasonable to
expect that LLDMS capacity to be first to curtail during emergencies that could otherwise force
unpaid customers offline. Therefore, Vistra supports utilization of the paid LLDMS capacity to
avoid firm load shed during transmission emergencies in addition to EEA events. However, as

Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                   Page 7
 noted above in response to Preamble Question #4, there are many conditions that must be put in
place around its appropriate use for transmission emergencies, since doing so can have other
market-distortive effects.

       To also limit interference with locational price signals in the wholesale market and to help
manage the “demand response fatigue” that can plague frequently-deployed loads, Vistra
recommends that the transmission emergency utilization be limited to actual transmission
emergencies (and not extended to anticipated transmission emergencies). This should help to strike
a balance between beneficial utilization and overburdening a subset of locationally valuable
flexible loads.

       Accordingly, Vistra recommends revising Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.521(d), (d)(1)(D),
(e)(2), and (e)(3)(A) as follows:

       (d)     Procurement. ERCOT may procure LLDMS from a large load customer on
       an as needed basis to help prevent an anticipated EEA event due to an extreme
       weather condition or alleviate an actual transmission emergency or EEA event due to
       an extreme weather condition.
                  […]
                  (D)    during a transmission emergency or an EEA event due to an extreme
                  weather condition.
       (e)        Deployment.
                  (1)    [no change]
                  (2)    ERCOT may deploy a large load customer as necessary to help
                  maintain reliability during an emergency EEA event due to an extreme
                  weather condition throughout the LLDMS obligation period.
                  (3)     When deployed by ERCOT, a large load customer must deploy
                  consistent with its obligations and must remain deployed:
                         (A)    for the duration of the emergency EEA event; or
                         (B)    until the large load customer can be recalled safely, as
                         determined and communicated by ERCOT.


c. Clarify that payments are for the LLDMS clearing price, not the wholesale energy price.

       Vistra generally disfavors out-of-market capacity programs for demand response in an
energy-only market, where demand should have a natural and intrinsic motivation to avoid market
costs – especially during times of scarcity. LLDMS, however, is required by statute so is not

Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                Page 8
 optional, and fortunately is at least required to offset its market-distortive impacts on price
formation. Still, it is important to note that LLDMS inherently provides a duplicative value by
providing both a capacity payment (LLDMS procurement payment) and the imputed avoided cost
of energy while curtailed. While Vistra has concerns with even the potentially duplicated value of
LLDMS being incongruent with the rest of the market construct, the competitive single clearing-
price procurement should discipline the clearing price.

       The only exchange of value contemplated within the rule is the LLDMS procurement
payment. Therefore, the logical reading of proposed paragraphs (f)(1)(C) & (D) is that they modify
the LLDMS market clearing price. Vistra is concerned, however, that proposed paragraphs (f)(1)(C)
& (D) could be misread as pancaking on a third valuation by also paying the curtailed load 25%
or 100% of the wholesale market clearing price for energy.

       To illustrate why this misreading is concerning, note that procurement offers under
proposed paragraph (d)(3)(B)(v) set a procurement limit of $5,000 per megawatt hour for LLDMS;
during peak scarcity conditions, the real-time wholesale price of energy may also reach
$5,000/MWh – the avoided cost of energy. This means that a curtailed LLDMS load would have
already received up to $10,000/MWh of intrinsic and extrinsic value from the curtailment – twice
the value afforded to generation resources and most of the other loads reacting to wholesale market
signals. Layering up to an additional $5,000/MWh based on the wholesale price of energy would
exacerbate that inequity by increasing the curtailed LLDMS load value to as much as
$15,000/MWh – thrice the value afforded to generation resources and most other loads reacting to
wholesale market signals.

       Therefore, Vistra recommends that 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C)-(D) be clarified to avoid any
doubt that it applies solely to the LLDMS market-clearing price:

       (f)     Payment and charges.
               (1)    ERCOT must pay a QSE that represents a large load customer
                      participating in LLDMS as follows:
                      (A)     all payments must be based on a single clearing price;
                      (B)     awards must be settled monthly after availability data is
                              confirmed;
                      (C)     A QSE representing a large load customer that is not instructed
                              by ERCOT to deploy but is subject to availability verification


Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                Page 9
                                    during the LLDMS obligation period may receive a payment
                                   based on 25% of the market clearing price for LLDMS; and
                          (D)      A QSE representing a large load customer that deploys
                                   consistent with ERCOT instructions during the LLDMS
                                   obligation period may receive payment based on 100% of the
                                   market clearing price for LLDMS associated with the
                                   deployed capacity.

        In the alternative, if Vistra misreads the proposed rule’s intent, then for the foregoing
reasons Vistra recommends striking proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C)-(D) and making other
conforming changes as follows:

        (f)      Payment and charges.
                 (1)      ERCOT must pay a QSE that represents a large load customer
                          participating in LLDMS as follows:
                          (A)      all payments must be based on a single clearing price; and
                          (B)      awards must be settled monthly after availability data is
                                   confirmed.;
                          (C)      A QSE representing a large load customer that is not instructed
                                   by ERCOT to deploy but is subject to availability verification
                                   during the LLDMS obligation period may receive a payment
                                   based on 25% of the market clearing price; and
                          (D)      A QSE representing a large load customer that deploys
                                   consistent with ERCOT instructions during the LLDMS
                                   obligation period may receive payment based on 100% of the
                                   market clearing price associated with the deployed capacity.


d. Recover the cost on a fixed, self-leveling $/MWh-basis fee across the year, not on an event
   basis.

        The proposed charge to loads based on the procurement period load ratio share could have
unintended consequences, including greater cost allocation to residential and other weather-
sensitive customers. Larger electricity customers are generally more likely to have contracts with
real-time market price exposure (whereas wholesale indexed residential prices are not permitted
by law), and during emergency conditions it is likely that many large loads will be curtailed under
PURA §§ 37.0561(e), 39.169(d), or 39.170(b).4 Thus, it is more likely that load ratio share


4
 i.e., including deployments under this proposed rule – making a potential fourth intrinsic value layer to the point
made in III.c above: avoiding LLDMS costs.


Vistra Comments on PFP
Project 58482                                                                                              Page 10
 allocation during a procurement period would over-allocate LLDMS costs to residential
customers.

          A more equitable and predictable cost recovery mechanism would be for ERCOT to
establish a fixed, self-leveling $/MWh fee across the calendar year. For instance, ERCOT’s
forecasted load for 2026 is 558,121,422 MWh.5 $54 million divided by that value yields
$0.09675/MWh. ERCOT could assess that on every MWh, using the accumulated balance as the
budget for the calendar year. If no procurements are made, the next year’s charge could drop to
zero. If actual load exceeds the load forecast, the charge could drop to zero even before year-end.
If load comes in below forecast, the procurement budget will simply continue to accumulate.

          This approach is also preferable for retail electric providers, because it is more predictable
to plan for a known program fee than take on unhedgeable risk that ERCOT may make a
spontaneous procurement/deployment (with a value potentially far exceeding the actual market
price for energy, as noted above).

          Accordingly, Vistra recommends revising Proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(3) as follows:

                  (3)     ERCOT must charge each load serving entity (LSE) for LLDMS
                          deployment costs based upon the LSE’s load ratio share a fixed dollar
                          per megawatt-hour basis during the procurement period calendar year.
                          If ERCOT accumulates more than the maximum established in
                          paragraph (4) below, ERCOT must suspend collection of the charge.


                                          IV.     CONCLUSION
          Vistra appreciates the Commission’ s consideration of these comments and looks forward
to working with the Commission, Staff, ERCOT, and other stakeholders toward adoption of a rule
that will foster economic development, maintain system reliability, faithfully implement the
Legislature’s objectives, and promote regulatory predictability.

                    VISTRA COMMENTS – EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


•   The curtailment directive in proposed 16 TAC §25.521(a)(1) should apply to loads not
    already otherwise curtailed and include statutory customer coordination language.
       o PURA §§ 37.0561(e), 39.169(d), and 39.170(b) can drive curtailments ahead of firm
         load shed. Duplicative load shed protocols and equipment are unnecessary and can be
         avoided with minor clarification.
       o PURA § 39.170(a) also requires the utility to confer with the customer to the extent
         feasible to shed load in a coordinated manner. The proposed rule had omitted this;
         Vistra recommends adding it in.


•   Limited deployments for actual transmission emergencies should be allowed for LLDMS.
       o A paid and pre-procured demand reduction may be better than firm load shed.
       o However, there are many conditions that must be put in place around its appropriate
         use for transmission emergencies, since doing so can have market-distortive effects.


•   Clarify that payments are for the LLDMS clearing price, not the wholesale energy price.
       o Language in proposed 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C)-(D) could be confused with providing
         a third payment value based on the wholesale energy price (in addition to the value of
         avoiding that price and value of the procurement clearing price).
       o This should be clarified; in the alternative, if 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(1)(C)-(D) were
         intended to provide a supplemental wholesale energy price-based payment, Vistra
         opposes that and recommends deleting subparagraphs (C) & (D).


•   Recover the cost on a fixed, self-leveling $/MWh-basis fee across the year, not on an event
    basis.
       o Revise 16 TAC § 25.521(f)(3) to require a predictable fixed $/MWh, subject to
         suspension if the fee accumulates more than $54M annual limit.

          The Commission should view the $54 million amount as a maximum expenditure cap
rather than a procurement target. ERCOT should procure only the amount of service necessary to
address identified reliability risks. Maintaining the proposed cap will allow the Commission and
stakeholders to evaluate actual program performance, participation, costs, and reliability benefits
before considering any future budget increases.

          Any proposal to increase the cap should be supported by demonstrated evidence that
additional expenditures would provide incremental and cost-effective reliability benefits to
ERCOT customers.

          Furthermore, as explained in greater detail below, the budget should be accumulated on a
self-leveling annual calendar year basis yielding a predictable $/MWh charge for Qualified
Scheduling Entities (QSEs) and Load Serving Entities (LSEs).


   3. What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
      far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

          ERCOT should assess anticipated extreme weather conditions and associated reliability
risks on a continual basis using its existing forecasting tools, but the decision to initiate an LLDMS
procurement should occur only when ERCOT determines there is a credible risk of an anticipated
emergency condition that will likely require deployment of the service.

          Consistent with the statutory requirement to provide at least 24 hours' notice, ERCOT
should initiate the auction sufficiently in advance to allow successful participants to prepare for a

 potential curtailment event while minimizing forecast uncertainty. Vistra recommends that
ERCOT conduct the auction approximately 24 to 48 hours before the anticipated deployment
period, with ERCOT retaining the flexibility to update procurement quantities as forecasts evolve.

         A procurement window too far in advance may result in over-procurement or procurement
based on weather forecasts that ultimately do not materialize. Conversely, a procurement
conducted too close to the anticipated event may limit participation and reduce the ability of
qualifying loads to safely prepare for curtailment. A 24-to-48-hour procurement window
appropriately balances forecast accuracy, operational preparedness, and competitive participation.
It would also naturally align with the 48-hour forecast review timeline in the Power Outage Alert
rule (16 TAC § 25.57).


    4. Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
       what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

         Vistra supports allowing ERCOT to deploy LLDMS during actual transmission
emergencies when demand reductions can meaningfully mitigate a material reliability threat.
However, the Commission should ensure that LLDMS remains a targeted emergency reliability
tool and is not used for routine congestion management or as a substitute for transmission planning.
ERCOT should be required to demonstrate that the transmission emergency presents a credible
risk to reliability, that existing operational tools are insufficient to address the condition, and that
any deployment is limited to the scope necessary to mitigate the emergency. This approach
preserves operational flexibility while protecting consumers from unnecessary program costs and
maintaining appropriate market incentives. In the comments below, Vistra recommends that
deployment for transmission emergencies be limited to actual transmission emergencies (and not
include anticipated emergencies).

         If the Commission allows ERCOT to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies, Vistra
advocates for the following guardrails:

    1.      Limit Deployments to Reliability Emergencies: LLDMS should only be used when a
            transmission event creates a credible risk of:

            •   Firm load shed,

            •   Cascading outages,

            •   Voltage instability, or
           •   Other significant reliability concerns.

        It should not be used for routine congestion management or economic dispatch issues.


   2.      Require Use of Existing Tools First: ERCOT should demonstrate that existing
           operational tools are insufficient before deploying LLDMS, including:
           •   Network reconfiguration,
           •   Outage management procedures,
           •   Existing emergency protocols.

        LLDMS should remain a tool of last resort.


   3.      Geographic Targeting: Deployments should be limited to the affected transmission-
           constrained area whenever practical, rather than triggering ERCOT-wide curtailments
           for localized problems.


   4.      Demonstrate Incremental Reliability Value: ERCOT should show that the requested
           demand reduction will materially reduce reliability risk and is not merely replacing
           transmission upgrades, planning activities, or normal operational practices.


   5.      Maintain Transparency: Following a deployment, ERCOT should provide stakeholders
           with:

           •   The nature of the transmission emergency,
           •   The amount of LLDMS procured and deployed,
           •   The reliability benefit achieved, and

           •   Why other tools were insufficient.


   6.      Protect Against Routine Use: The Commission should make clear that transmission
           emergency deployments are intended to be exceptional circumstances, not a recurring
           operational tool. Frequent use could indicate underlying transmission planning or
           infrastructure deficiencies that should be addressed through other processes.

c. Clarify that payments are for the LLDMS clearing price, not the wholesale energy price.

        Vistra generally disfavors out-of-market capacity programs for demand response in an
energy-only market, where demand should have a natural and intrinsic motivation to avoid market
costs - especially during times of scarcity. LLDMS, however, is required by statute so is not

of energy while curtailed. While Vistra has concerns with even the potentially duplicated value of
LLDMS being incongruent with the rest of the market construct, the competitive single clearing-
price procurement should discipline the clearing price.

       To illustrate why this misreading is concerning, note that procurement offers under

wholesale market signals.

real-time market price exposure (whereas wholesale indexed residential prices are not permitted
by law), and during emergency conditions it is likely that many large loads will be curtailed under
PURA §§ 37.0561(e), 39.169(d), or 39.170(b).4 Thus, it is more likely that load ratio share

         A more equitable and predictable cost recovery mechanism would be for ERCOT to
establish a fixed, self-leveling $/MWh fee across the calendar year. For instance, ERCOT's
forecasted load for 2026 is 558,121,422 MWh.5 $54 million divided by that value yields

zero. If actual load exceeds the load forecast, the charge could drop to zero even before year-end.
If load comes in below forecast, the procurement budget will simply continue to accumulate.

to plan for a known program fee than take on unhedgeable risk that ERCOT may make a
spontaneous procurement/deployment (with a value potentially far exceeding the actual market
price for energy, as noted above).
